title: Prayer and medicine
hookLine: Judaism values both doctors and prayer
tomorrow: Saba's home, and Mom hasn't slept. who takes care of the carer?

lines: WHICH ONE IS DOING THE HEALING?
cards: Two screens open at once. One is a patient portal: surgery Tuesday, arrive at six, nothing to eat after midnight. The other is the family chat, where an aunt has written: praying for you!!!
So which one is doing the healing? Inside Jewish tradition, two serious voices answer that question differently, and both quote the Bible.

teach.b: The first voice remembers King Asa. The book of Chronicles says that when he fell ill, "yet in his disease he sought not to the LORD, but to the physicians."
Nachmanides, the medieval commentator, wrote that in a time when people lived fully close to God, they wouldn't need doctors at all.
Its best case: healing comes from God in the end, and a waiting room can make you forget that.
The second voice starts in Exodus, in a law about an injury: the one who caused it must see that the injured person is thoroughly healed.

The Talmud, in Bava Kamma, reads that line and says: from here, the doctor is given permission to heal. Maimonides was himself a physician. Later law codes go further and call healing a mitzvah, a commandment.
Its best case: the body is a gift, and neglecting it is no kind of faith.

teach.h: INSTEAD OF, OR AS WELL AS?
teach.b: Notice what the first voice is really worried about: Asa sought the doctors instead of God, not as well as. And Jewish practice, as it's lived, mostly holds both together.

teach.h: THE SURGEON, AND A MI SHEBERAKH.

teach.b: The community says a prayer called the Mi Sheberakh, asking for a refuah shleimah, a complete healing, of body and of spirit.
Something to tell a friend tonight: the Talmud finds the doctor's permission to heal inside a law about a fistfight.

how: Jews seek medical care, which later codes of Jewish law call a mitzvah, and in synagogue a Mi Sheberakh prayer is often said for the sick by name, asking for a complete healing of body and spirit.

o: a rule that only a rabbi may decide on surgery
choosing prayer first, and doctors as a last resort
seeking doctors and praying, held together

games.q: two voices on healing — tap the pairs.
p: sought the physicians, not the LORD
a sage who was a physician

s: Jewish tradition says faith means avoiding doctors
the Talmud gives the doctor permission to heal, and later codes call healing a mitzvah.
the Talmud finds the permission to heal in a law about an injury
Exodus says the one who caused it must see the injured thoroughly healed.
the complaint against King Asa is that he saw doctors at all
the verse says he sought the physicians instead of the LORD: instead of, not as well as.

games.q: you lean hard toward the doctors' side. a friend asks: "what's the strongest case for the other view?" what do you say?
o: healing comes from God in the end, and medicine can make us forget it.
doctors are usually wrong, so prayer is the safer bet.
prayer works faster than medicine if you believe enough.
games.why: that's the heart of the Asa and Nachmanides view. the tradition as lived holds both: see the surgeon, and say the Mi Sheberakh.

practice: Name one health task you've been putting off: a checkup, a refill, a dentist, a walk your body keeps asking for. Then name what's in the way. Then choose one small first step, and when you'll take it.

wordCard.voice: Prayer and medicine: the surgeon's hands and the community's prayer, held together. The Talmud gives the doctor permission; the Mi Sheberakh asks for complete healing.

orig.note: Hebrew: a complete healing. what people wish the sick, and what the Mi Sheberakh asks for.

carryVoice: Pocket this one: doctors and prayer, as well as, not instead of. Wishing a refuah shleimah to anyone who needs one.
